explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is, friend! The text says Hezekiah reigns there twenty-nine years (2 Kings 18:2). Home base settled. If you picked it, you're already ahead of me, because I once lost my own bakery's front door and I'm not even moving.

Fair guess, friend, because Samaria is in this passage. It's Israel's capital, though, and it shows up later when the Assyrians come marching. Hezekiah is king of Judah, and the text says he reigns in Jerusalem. Hold on to Samaria, because we're going back there.

Bethel doesn't show up anywhere in these verses, friend. The text says Hezekiah reigns in Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:2). That's where he runs Judah. So many city names in one passage, it's like a whole tray of cookies and nobody labeled the flavors.

True! The text says, "And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done." Think about that for a second, friend. A whole kingdom to run, and what the writer wants us to know first is that he did right in God's eyes.

Not quite, friend, and I'm glad we get to fix it. The text says, "And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father David had done." Right there in verse 3, no hedging. It's the first thing we learn about how Hezekiah ran his kingdom.

That's it, friend! The text says he "cut down the Asherah poles." That's three jobs in a row: removing, shattering, cutting. This man doesn't do half a job. I once left a batch in the oven for one extra minute and called it a day, so I respect the thoroughness.

Gold paint, friend? That's a redecorating plan, and Hezekiah isn't redecorating. The text says he "cut down the Asherah poles." Removing the high places, shattering the pillars, and cutting these down is a full cleanup, no paint involved.

Moving them indoors is like sliding the burnt batch to the back of the cupboard and hoping nobody notices. Hezekiah doesn't hide anything, friend. The text says he "cut down the Asherah poles." Down means down.

Close, friend, but the text says the opposite. Hezekiah "demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made." Moses, Israel's leader, made it long before, so it had history. It wasn't tucked away safe, though. It was demolished.

False is right, friend! There's no safekeeping here. The text says Hezekiah "demolished the bronze snake called Nehushtan that Moses had made." Moses, Israel's leader, made it back in the wilderness (Numbers 21:9), and still it came down in Hezekiah's day.

explanations.answer: People had been burning incense to it
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, friend. "For up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it." The snake itself came from Moses, Israel's leader, but the people were burning incense to it, so Hezekiah demolished it. Worth noticing that even something with that kind of history didn't get a pass.

explanations.answer: It had cracked beyond any repair
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the text says the snake was cracked, friend. The reason is right there in verse 4: "for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it." That's what the writer tells us. I'd have blamed a cracked pan, but that's me.

explanations.answer: The king of Assyria wanted it
explanations.explanation: The king of Assyria doesn't come into this one, friend. The text gives the reason: "for up to that time the Israelites had burned incense to it." Assyria shows up later in the passage, and it's not about the snake. Nobody was bidding on this thing.

True! The text says, "No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him." Before AND after, friend. That's a long line of kings, and the writer says none of them were like Hezekiah. Right after, it tells us why that's said: he trusted in the LORD.
The text says otherwise, friend. Verse 5 says, "No king of Judah was like him, either before him or after him." That covers kings from both directions. Hezekiah stands out in a very long line.

Not this time, friend. The text says, "He remained faithful to the LORD and did not turn from following Him." There's no turning away in these verses. He kept the commandments the LORD had given Moses, Israel's leader, and that's how the text describes him.

False is right, friend! The text says, "He remained faithful to the LORD and did not turn from following Him." No part-time following here. It also says he kept the commandments the LORD had given Moses, Israel's leader.

Serve! The text says Hezekiah "rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him." That's the king of a powerful empire, and Hezekiah says no. And remember, the verse right before it says the LORD was with Hezekiah.

Visit makes it sound like Hezekiah just skipped a coffee date, friend. The text is stronger than that: he "rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him." This was a rebellion, not a scheduling conflict. The word is serve.
Meet is a little too casual, friend. Hezekiah wasn't dodging a meeting. The text says he "rebelled against the king of Assyria and refused to serve him." He wasn't being rude, he was rebelling.

The Philistines, friend! The text says, "He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders, from watchtower to fortified city." Watchtower to fortified city. That's a whole stretch of land, not just one corner. Prospering wherever he went, exactly like verse 7 says.

The Moabites don't show up in these verses, friend. The text says, "He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders." Plenty of nations in the Bible, and it's easy to grab the wrong one. Keep your eyes on the Philistines this time.

Edomites are a good Bible name, friend, but not the one in this verse. The text says, "He defeated the Philistines as far as Gaza and its borders, from watchtower to fortified city." The answer is right there in verse 8.
Years is right, friend. The text says, "And at the end of three years, the Assyrians captured it." Three years of siege. That's a long time, and I think it's a heavy part of the story.

The text counts longer than months, friend. It says, "And at the end of three years, the Assyrians captured it." Three years of siege on Samaria, Israel's capital. I think this part of the story is a heavy one.

Weeks would be much shorter than what the text says, friend. The siege lasted three years: "And at the end of three years, the Assyrians captured it." This is a heavy part of the story, so let's slow down and get it right.

Not Egypt, friend. The text says, "The king of Assyria exiled the Israelites to Assyria and settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes." So the exile is to Assyria and those places. This is a heavy moment in the story.

False is right, friend. The text says, "The king of Assyria exiled the Israelites to Assyria and settled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes." Egypt isn't named here. It's a heavy moment, so I'm glad we got the details right.

explanations.answer: They would not listen to the LORD or obey
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives, friend. "This happened because they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God, but violated His covenant." It adds that they "would neither listen nor obey." I think this one hurts, and it's good the writer says plainly why.

explanations.answer: Their city walls were built too low
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't mentioned anywhere in this passage, friend. The reason is stated in verse 12: "they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God, but violated His covenant." That's what the writer says. It's a heavy part of the story, and I'd rather stick to what the text gives.

explanations.answer: Their army was too small to fight back
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions the size of their army, friend. It tells us the reason: "they did not listen to the voice of the LORD their God, but violated His covenant." They "would neither listen nor obey." I think this is a sad part of the story, and the text is clear about why.
